title: What’s your feeling on gluttony of biopics flooding cinema the last decade or so?

commenti.body: [removed]

I skip almost all of them. Most historical figures, even interesting ones, aren't actually compelling enough to be the subject of a feature film without a lot of fudging on the history. And even then, these films tend to be somewhat formulaic and inherently uninteresting to me.

This goes double for biopics about anyone living. The dust hasn't settled and the history is still being written. In the case of political leaders the really juicy primary sources may not even be public yet, and won't be for decades. Making films about living public figures feels doubly uninteresting as a result.

I don’t understand their appeal. If I want to know about a real person I’d read about them. Few of these movies show much more than an encyclopedia or Wikipedia entry.

I think it’s just that people don’t read much nowadays, and the way celebrities have become the cultural elite, as aristocrats, the wealthy, and artists were in the past, and so people want to see ‘their betters’ to partake in their lives vicariously.

I don't actively avoid them but I never seek them out either. And if anything, they're more often than not dryly to poorly directed and uncompelling and, in a word, sappy (Elivs, Bohemian Rhapsody,) which gives me less of an incentive. Not to mention most if not all are full of misleading details, with some, like The Disaster Artist, going out of their way to add things just for the sake of it.

I'm not against the idea of a biopic, but I find that there's no good examples of one that actually is a biopic. The most seem like a salesman's lies to get me into buying a brand image -- propaganda.
[removed]

Well, the first thing I'd want to know is: has there *really* been an especially large glut of them in the last decade? There have always been middlebrow pseudo-prestige biopics, but have there actually been more of them lately? I'd want to know what the breakdown of genres looks like, and how that's changed over time

Assuming, then, that it is true that there's been an influx, I think the explanation would probably be the boring one that explains whatever% of the industry, viz. producers following success. Once a few biopics become successful, they make a bunch more, some of which are also successful, so they make even more, some of which are also successful, so etc
I forgot to mention that nearly all of these are grossly miscast, like it’s an industry in-joke that they cast actors who in no way with physically or essentially resemble the subject in any way.
As for the halcyon days of when movies were challenging etc, I dunno, the majority of popular films have always been stuff like Hey Hey in the Hayloft and Ants in Your Plants of 1939

It certainly seems like I see and hear more about them being made and very much marketed towards playing up nostalgic impulses in people. It’s just about spectacle now. The days of the Frances Farmer’s and Karen Silkwood’s are seemingly long gone in terms of modestly scaled, sobering biopics. 

But there’s got to be a dimension of this that includes the absolute thrill of people seeing scenes/costumes/events recreated on screen with actors from the lives of public figures they might be fascinated by. The actual images and sounds of them in reality aren’t enough, they crave seeing a facsimile, a pure surface image, of the lives of someone who they might project upon.

I view biopics as the reality shows of the film world.  Easy because you don't have to create a story or characters and guaranteed money-makers because most people seem to have questionable tastes.  If I'm interested in someone's life story, I'd rather read a book about them instead of a dramatic interpretation. 

I've not seen Oppenheimer. I heard nothing but good things about it, but it just doesn't seem interesting to me.  

That being said, I absolutely love The Motorcycle Diaries. It doesn't play like a typical biopic, and it's very well done.

Biopics are usually not very interesting and pretty conventional. That's not to say they can never be entertaining, but they are rarely surprising and the worst ones follow a boring formula. I love Amy Winehouse but I really have zero interest in watching movie about her  because it's just going to be another mediocre rehash.

How's that? DDL in Lincoln was fine. I know Baron Cohen was supposed to play Freddie Mercury prior to Malek who both, while not particularly great choices, resemble him enough. The Disaster Artist was Franco's pet project so it's really more on himself, on both senses. Also Seymour Hoffman with Capote, who I consider a great choice.

I think 2 of clownish examples I can think of is the creepy casting of Gary Oldman for Mank and Leo for Catch Me If You Can whose scam Spielberg openly embraced for some similarly fudged reason. Maybe the in-joke is a hit or miss?

Cohen would never have been allowed to play a man of color in 2017, even if he didn’t age out. Malek looked enough like him but he botched that voice and didn’t capture Freddie’s dynamism. For Capote, I thought Tony Jones did the role better and looked the part too.

I’m still baffled at the enormous praise Austin Butler got/gets for Elvis. The fact he was even able to get into a room to audition for it is shocking. Physically all wrong and the essence of that man is replaced by a one note void that Butler brings to each scene. 

There’s countless examples of either the actors physicality or essence being completely ill-suited for the star they’re playing. It’s only getting worse.

I rarely want to watch  a biopic. 

Double down on that if the person is a modern well documented person where you can make a great documentary. 

I don’t need a Lance Armstrong biopic, when you can make an incredible documentary with contemporary interviews. 

As you go back in history I am a little more open to  like an Alexander the Great movie.

i think they appeal to the common viewer because they're "safe" serious films. they operate largely on tropes, they rarely paint outside of the lines narratively, while giving more room for artistry than your average marvel film.

I upvoted you initially cause I was 100% sure it was sarcasm. Still I respect your opinion even if it is hard for me to comprehend. How can real life be less interesting than super heroes fighting for the mucguffin of the day?

Not sarcasm.

To be clear, I find real life *extremely* interesting. History is one of my passions and was my major in undergrad. I consider myself a lifelong student of history, political science, geopolitics, global affairs, etc. And I enjoy historical fiction, on film and in other mediums. Historical epics are one of my favorite subgenres of film. And I like stories that are drawn from current events, if handled with subtlety and coming from writers who actually know what they're talking about.

I just don't think most public figures, the people themselves, are interesting enough to be *the centerpiece of a two hour plus* ***biopic****.* Certainly not public figures who are still living, when so much of their story is often yet to be researched.

I also think the subjects that are sometimes chosen for biopics, while interesting people, don't necessarily make interesting protagonists for film as a visual medium. Just because someone had an interesting life doesn't mean it's going to make for a good movie. Just because it might make for a few dynamic or interesting scenes, doesn't mean there's enough actually there for a compelling feature film.

I'm up for it, especially if you can come up with an original film narrative, and not rely on the standard formula. Like I can't wait for the up comedy GG Allin bipoc from the director of the Mayhem biopic, Lords Of Chaos where everybody came off like a shit head. I have to imagine Merle Allin Jr. was consulted on it the mostly for accuracy. I've read a late 80's autobiography GG wrote, and some stuff take with a grain of salt, because he lived his persona 24/7, but he was married, had a series of straight jobs, and lost every possession in an apartment fire. After that, it's easy to see how he became more detached from everyone and accepted traveling with the clothes on his back and making enough money for booze and bail money for the rest of his life. It's going to be a very transgressive biopic.

They can be good films, but one of the thing that bothers me about biopics are scenes where there’s dialogue between people that makes me think “did this conversation even happen or did the writers just make this up?” It kinda ruins it for me because I then believe that majority of it is over sensationalized. As you stated, they seem like easy cash grabs. 

On a similar note, I have a bone to pick with comic book/video game adaptations. The source material is already there, and then a movie/show is created, which is cool and fun, but it seems to me that there isn’t much originality coming from big Hollywood movies. 

So, I’ve been sticking to my criterion subscription and looking for films with more substance and originality.

The worst thing about modern biopics is that they come decades too early with the subjects of the film being consulting or even producer credits. Ensures we get the blandest, saddest, least interesting version of all of those stories. Bohemian Rhapsody is just the most prominent example. Of this JLo shit. These projects are artistically dead.  Basically just commercials for how great someone is or was.

The explosion of biopics about musicians is being driven by Sony buying up artist’s back catalogs and producing films about the artist to boost record sales. 

The Elton John, Whitney Houston, Bob Marley, Amy Winehouse and Queen movies are all because of this. 

This was exacerbated by the pandemic, when some artists missed much expected touring income and sold off their music to make up for it, like Bruce Springsteen. 

The films about Elvis and Priscilla Presley are also direct results of Lisa Marie passing and the remaining family being more amiable about biopics than she was. 

Since these ones are basically just long form ads, I feel they end up being pretty toothless and one dimensional, but it’s fun to see which actors can also sing?

To me Oppenheimer worked better than your average biopic because it depicted the process of engineering in a compelling way. Often I see biopics that have to resort to just telling rather than showing the audience what makes the central figure interesting. One commenter noted that famous historical figures often lead pretty conventional lives. Even if they're known for some groundbreaking intellectual breakthrough, it's hard to dramatize a creative genius just sitting around a typewriter or a piano or whatever, coming up with their breakthrough. And at least in Oppenheimer, the development of the bomb was a large collaborative feat involving multiple contributors who made for interesting characters in their own right and Nolan was genuinely interested in the process of how a nuclear bomb works and how it was theorized and then brought into being. 

On the other hand Maestro was, to me, what's generally wrong with biopics: it doesn't really investigate Bernstein's approach to music and what makes him an interesting figure and instead focuses on his interpersonal life and how he mistreated his wife and family because he couldn't come out. I mean it's fine but that story could probably have been told about many closeted men who lived during that time. Also the movie felt the need to cover his entire life (except of course his artistic process) so it has that flattened, shapeless narrative that most lives have. And also it just reeks of vanity project.  You can tell Bradley Cooper just did this so he could get footage of himself conducting an orchestra, and that he "identifies" so much with Bernstein because they're both such "geniuses" in their own right.
“But they weren't about tramps, lockouts, sweatshops, people eating garbage in alleys and living in piano boxes and ash cans.”

I always laugh at people who thought that *Catch Me If You Can* was meant to be a serious autobiography. It's a caper movie about a juvenile imposter. The film took so many liberties from the loosely based book that it has been regarded as pure fiction since its release. Funny that I never hear those complaints about *Fargo*.

I’m someone who isn’t wild about biopics in general, but I think you’re fighting a steep uphill battle in dismissing the casting of PSH as Capote. In my mind it’s one of the most universally beloved portrayals of this century.

That’s a solid casting and solid movie, but I’m just saying I think it was done technically better elsewhere. I’m more pissy about these grand spectacles of bigger pop names where the person centralized isn’t given any genuine insight into their selfhood, largely because most of these movies are made by a committee and not a singular artist collecting all the facets they know of the subject accrued over the years and connecting dots of their psychology.
[removed]
You're saying "technically better." Are you saying they did a better job of "copying" the real guy? Because I hate when they just cast someone based off looks and voice.

Love and Mercy, the Brian Wilson Biopic starring Paul Dano and John Cusack, is the best biopic I can think of to recent memory. I think what makes it as good as it is are a number of things, perhaps the largest being the actual Brian Wilson’s fairly egoless attitude towards approving/cleaning up any parts of the movie about his personal life. 

The movie itself isn’t a “greatest hits” of his catalogue/career, but more a very close examination of Wilson’s life and personhood shown in creating his opus in the 60’s with Pet sounds, and his subsequent mental health struggles, jumping forward to the 80’s examining him then as he begins a relationship with his future wife while under the abuse of his psychologist and conservator.

It is an incredibly human film about a person who happens to be a critically acclaimed and highly influential artist rather than the other way around, which is where I think a lot of these modern biopics trip up.
does disaster artist really count as biopic? I took it as a loose artistic interpretation of the making of the Room

Back in the 60s 2001: A Space Odyssey, The Graduate, Gone with the Wind, The Apartment Lawrence of Arabia, To Kill a Mockingbird, and Doctor Zhivago were top grossing movies in America. Sure, the James Bond movies were very popular, there were light hearted musicals, and maybe Planet of the Apes the year it was release. However, everything changed in the post Star Wars era. We get escapism alone, now.

Fair points, and I know people always say that kind of thing about pre-/post- Jaws; I still feel it's easy to look back with rose-coloured glasses and focus on the good stuff and ignore the majority of crap. On the other hand, I just looked at a list of the 50 top-grossing films of the 2010s and, yeeeeesh

[https://m.imdb.com/list/ls026040906/](https://m.imdb.com/list/ls026040906/) There's the top 50 grossing movies worldwide. Every single one without even a single exception is a type of fantasy, action movie, or kids movie. There is literally not one exception which is amazing. The American box office is basically the same with the only difference being one horror movie (IT) and American Sniper are on the list [http://www.boxofficereport.com/domestic2010s.html](http://www.boxofficereport.com/domestic2010s.html)
yeah to my memory this style of movie has been a constant presence for decades. one reason I've always heard is that it sets up the lead for an Oscar run
Yep, that's the one I was looking at. what a depressing list!

hardly a blip on my radar since i just ignore them & let them blow by me w/o even a second glance in their direction. that said, i am extremely glad that Elvis (2022) exists, & that i randomly decided to watch it, because it is a baffling artifact that really endeared itself to me in a way i never would’ve imagined

I like the subject of your post, but I disagree with your premise; I do not think there has been a deluge or increase in the number of biopics in the last decade or so. They've always cranked them out like crazy. I think there has been an uptick in musician biopics, and those are the worst. Those are coming out because the studios are lazy and think they can make a quick buck. I'm not sure where the niche "musician biopic" genre truly starts, but my first notable experience was probably Oliver Stone's *The Doors*; which was a brilliantly crafted pile of doodoo. Val Kilmer is exquisite and the filmmaking is *incredible*, but when I revisited that film I couldn't help but think of it as a useless exercise in masturbatory pulp. Then you get very competent entries like *Ray* that do a decent job encapsulating the important chapters of the subject's life and importance to music and culture, but still leave me fairly cold. I think these films fail because they are taking an artist's life and telling a "by the numbers" story straight down the middle, and I think they only kind of work as a celebration as opposed to an examination.

I respect people who don't enjoy biopics *period*, but I disagree. I think there are plenty of important stories of historical figures that are wonderfully realized through film. But that raises another question: is there a distinction between a film based on a historical figure and a biopic, and what is that distinction? Is *Schindler's List* a biopic? *Braveheart*? *The Imitation Game*? *Lawrence of Arabia*?

I think there are some biopics that stand as the absolute pinnacle of filmmaking. *Ghandi* is something every person should watch at least once. *Malcolm X* may be the best and most important biopic ever made. I absolutely loved *Oppenheimer*. I think what matters is this: why was this person important to their time, and why should we care about it today. *Ghandi* came out at a time (...similar to today) where violence was being promoted as a legitimate tool for international political negotiations and struggles. *Malcolm X* famously opens with the Rodney King footage. *Oppenheimer* coincidentally came out at a time when the use of tactical nuclear weapons is actually being debated and global superpowers are aggressively posturing and engaging in proxy wars. The tricky part here is that none of these examples seem to be the most artful examples of what film can be, but they are great examples of how popular film is in dialogue with social fears, concerns, and needs.

I think a great biopic can help us understand something about humanity, the individual subject, and how their place in history matters to the present. I think a lot of them, like many other films, are uninspired cash grabs.
I love Freddy Mercury from my fingertips to my bone marrow, and that is why I will never watch *Bohemian Rhapsody*
Holy shit that makes so much sense

A lot of them are a drag, because they are about just this person, and don't have a message that directly impacts the audience - always very well-acted, but what was Elvis trying to say? Or Bohemian Rhapsody? Or Ray? The whole message is that they we're important to culture. But how is that metaphorical, how is that dramatic, and why should we care?

Obviously there are exceptions but I agree with you. Historical FICTION is much more interesting. Creativity is the fuel of film, and frankly, you can't win this race by committee. One person is making decisions at a particular time. Can you imagine if the Director held a vote on set whenever they needed to decide something? Point is, story is the most popular entertainment on earth because it takes us away. Every time you have anything on your mind but an idea that is uniquely yours, then your movie has failed its goal.

They feel weird to me because they almost always just feel like a cash grab. 

Either the subject is still alive, and it's a grandiose celebration of them, or they have passed and it's uncomfortably personal, about their demons/social problems that people feel what propelled them to stardom.

The only modern “biopic” that asked those questions, that breached convention, was Todd Haynes’ “I’m Not There”, where he not only illuminates the many facets of Dylan but says something about the breadth of a nation and a world that manifested what he gave back to it.

You bring up an excellent point that I hadn’t considered, of taking people who passed away some time before the movie is made and recontextualizing who they were for an updated sensibility. The filmmakers making these are by and large not “artists”, they’re not following a profound, singular vision where they truly and often abstractly understand who this person was and what made them stick in the collective consciousness. 

Take the new Amy Winehouse movie. I’m a huge fan of hers and haven’t seen the movie yet, but it’s very fair to say from all I read that it completely sands down the darkest shadows of her inner and outer worlds, defers blame off the family, and gives us a portrait of just a naughty girl who was simply impossible. But the issue of her addictions and mental illness (BPD), that she even HAD a mental illness, is something that in 2007-2011 was widely mocked in a disgusting way that now people are at least acting like is a serious thing (or maybe now it’s the younger generations coming of age and seeing the horrible morality of their elders). The treatment of what she went through is likely seen in the film from a 2024 standpoint, giving her essence and life a framework for a time after she died and throughly missing pieces that you need to have her self cohere on screen.

There's something else that needs to be factored in though. Nowadays everyone has a pretty good setup at home. If you are a frequent movie-watcher, and watch a lot of "smart" movies (however you classify that) you are probably watching most of them at home, and only going to the theatre for movies that benefit from that experience - loud action movies where it's not a bad thing if the audience laughs or cheers.

In the 1960s, the theatre was the only way to watch any movie, and action movies generally sucked because we didn't have the special effects to make them credible.

It's easy to say that and while I see what you're saying, nobody has provided evidence that's true for many people; I understand it's true for a small minority of film buffs, probably like yourself and me. Ackshually (pardon me, lol) I find it's still very hard to find Bergman, Tarkovsky or someone like that without using piracy. If you don't pirate, you're probably ordering expensive blu rays that take a couple weeks deliver, I guess. Basically there's no empirical proof that many people are doing what you're suggesting, but the box office is empirical proof, of something, at least.

If you want more empiricial evidence, here's Netflix's top movies:

[https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/canada](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/canada)

It's also driven home even more when you look at Netflix's top 10 tv shows. That's especially in light of this supposedly being the prestiege drama era:

[https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/tv](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/tv)

It doesn't account fully for it, but it accounts some. People seeking those movies are also likely to get them from the library.

And there is another huge driving factor. If you want a smart movie, you are going to draw from the last 100 years of history. If you want a blockbuster, it's almost always going to be something recent. The people looking for those types of movies will always be steered into one of a few titles at any given time.
[removed]

I think it shows that we're living in a time with a lot of strife and unhappiness, when the majority of people are unhappy with the direction the world seems to be going in, and so people are hungry for films that let them escape into a "better" past. That includes biopics that present an overly-rosy picture of famous individuals who already have a generally positive public reputation.

I think this sums it up well, to extract the essence from the complex layers of their appeal and the cultural mood. I’m not saying escapism and fluffy stuff shouldn’t be loved, but it needs to be in an appropriate context.

This seems to be becoming more and more of a problem with bio-docs, too, where either the subject themselves or their family/estate get a production credit and some degree of script approval to go with it - especially when there's money to be made off the subject's legacy/brand, which is why we see so much of this with music bio-pics.

I feel that biopics are some of the easiest movies that can be made. Telling the story of a person’s life is not hard. You just have to get the right people and the right studio to tell that story. However I do feel that the reason we are seeing a lot more of these films is because Hollywood is scared to try to get any new concept in film. So they’re going to keep churning out these biopics and making sequels because they know it’s a winning formula. And if the person they’re making the biopic on is popular enough it’ll generate enough revenue at the box office to make it all worth it
